A classical effect of electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) is demonstrated in a planar metamaterial in the ultraviolet regime.
The EIT unit cell consists of a vertical cut wire as the bright resonator and two horizontal cut wire pairs as the dark element.
The destructive interference between the two resonance paths leads to an EIT-like transmission spectrum of the metamaterial.
The frequency absorption band of the sawtooth anisotropic metamaterial infrared absorber has a FWHM of 86% at normal incidence with over 95% absorbing efficiency.
The broadband infrared absorber based on an array of nanostrip antennas of different sizes has the largest bandwidth for efficient absorption of light reported in the literature.
The plasmonic super absorber etched on a gold film can provide broadband and polarization-independent resonant light absorption over the entire visible spectrum with an averaged absorption above 90%.
An arbitrarily thin metamaterial layer can perfectly absorb or giantly amplify an incident plane wave at a critical angle when the real parts of the permittivity and permeability are zero.
Metamaterial absorbers are used to construct terahertz modulators by incorporating amorphous silicon, where the conductivity change modulates the absorption and reflected wave amplitude.
The planar terahertz magnetic metamaterial is made up of periodic dual layer spirals and is extremely sub-wavelength in size.
The contrast between the transmission peak and dip in the EIT-like phenomenon was further enhanced by incorporating the Fabry-Perot resonance effect.
The broadband slow-wave absorbers can be utilized in the application fields of photovoltaic devices, thermal emitters, and high-responsivity broadband detectors.

Zero-index metamaterials can be used for the development of ultra-thin absorbers and amplifiers, with potential applications in magnetic resonance imaging, electromagnetic wave absorption, THz radiation control, and subwavelength imaging.

Future research directions include experimentally realizing the EIT-like phenomenon and exploring its sensor applications, extending the working frequency of the broadband absorbers to terahertz, and further exploiting the properties and applications of zero-index metamaterials.
The research results in this project have been published in high-impact journals such as Nano Letters (impact factor over 12) and Applied Physics Letters.
The project was funded by the AOARD (AOARD-114045) and aimed to study optical slow-wave metamaterial structures and explore their tunability and applications.
